The Commit Book · Basketball How to use this
How to use this playbook
Read chapter one before you spend anything. Then work the dated plan in chapter two with your
school counsellor and the athlete's club coach, one line at a time, crossing off the "done when" tests. Chapters
three to six are reference: what the paperwork means, what to send, what film has to look like, and what it all costs.
The one idea in this book
A family that knows the roster limit, the signing formula and the film standard competes with families that have
a bigger camp budget. Most of what a $5,000 service sells you is scheduling and follow-through; the rules, the dates
and the questions are free, and almost nobody writes them down. That is the whole argument for a plan on paper.

Three things that surprised families last year
The National Letter of Intent no longer exists. Division I eliminated it in October 2024 and
Division II followed within weeks. The site that ran it for sixty years went dark on 1 May 2025. What you sign now
is a school's written offer of athletics aid . Anything you read that says "sign your NLI" is a year out of date,
including your own coach's advice.
In Division I the number that binds a coach is a roster limit, not a scholarship limit. At
settlement schools, fifteen players in the program, funded or not. A coach can hold fifteen people and fund six.
Grassroots events are gated. A Division I coach may only evaluate at NCAA-certified events.
The league, not the parent, is responsible for that. Ask before you pay.
The Commit Book · Basketball 1 · Roster math
1. Roster math before anything else
Every plan in this book follows from one question: how many players can a team actually carry, and how many of
them can it pay? Basketball answers it more brutally than almost any other sport, because the roster is small, the
participation pool is enormous, and the aid is almost never full.
Level
What the limit is now
What that means for your list
D1, settlement school
15 people in the program, aid not capped and not guaranteed. Previously 13 for men, 15 for women.
Ask how many of the 15 will be funded next year, and whether one is held for your position group.
"How many scholarships do you have" is the wrong question.
D1, non-settlement
No national roster law; the conference or the school sets it.
Ask the same question. The answer may be a conference rule, and a coach who cannot answer it is telling you something.
D2
10 equivalencies for the whole squad.
Offers are usually halves and thirds. Compare real cost, not prestige.
D3
No athletic aid at all.
The offer is an admissions decision plus an institutional aid package. The coach can advocate, not pay.
NAIA
8 scholarships. No recruiting calendar, no evaluation restriction, no enforced letter of intent.
Lowest academic bar and the most direct coach contact, but the paperwork binds you to nothing and to everything at once. Read the school's own paper.
NJCAA
15 scholarships, one academic year per sport, one letter of intent that closes every other JUCO door.
A genuine second path with transfer credit, and the one route where a late bloomer can rebuild a class year.
The odds, in the NCAA's own numbers
Of 540,704 high-school boys players, 3.6% reach any NCAA school: 1.1% at
Division I, 1.1% at Division II, 1.5% at Division III. Across all high-school athletes in every sport,
about 2% receive any athletic aid. Count the doors from the other direction and there were 1,187
first-year students at D1, 988 at D2 and 897 at D3: 61% of the doors are D2 and D3. The NCAA publishes
both figures and most families have seen only the first.
So what the plan looks like
Build the list for the doors you can actually reach and treat Division I as the upside.
A realistic basketball list is roughly 8 to 12 Division I programs where you have a position-group
case, 10 to 15 Division II , 10 to 15 Division III where the academic fit and the aid
package work, 5 to 10 NAIA , and 3 to 5 JUCO programs you would genuinely attend if the spring
went sideways. Anything narrower is a wish, not a plan.

Four questions that turn "we're interested" into a number
How many of the 15 will be funded next year, and how many are held for my position group?
Is there room for me at the roster limit you submit in December, or does someone ahead of me have to leave?
What would have to be true for you to write the aid down on or after 1 August?
If I sign in November, what happens to my aid in year two?
Questions one and two are legal to ask and answerable under the settlement rules. A coach who answers them is
recruiting you; one who changes the subject is telling you where you are on the board, and that is worth more than
a compliment.
The Commit Book · Basketball 4 · What to send
4. What to send, and when
Who presses send. The athlete, from the athlete's address, with the high-school coach copied.
Coaches will not always say it, and NAIA coaches say it plainly: if a parent writes, they assume nobody can read.
The parent's job is the paperwork and the deadline, not the inbox.
The subject line. Class year, position, height, GPA, town, and one number that matters:
2029 PG | 6'2" | 3.6 GPA | 14.1 PPG | Pewaukee, WI - film inside
The body. Under 180 words, in the player's own voice. One honest sentence on why this school.
The film link and the data block. One ask. No attachments. Send it, then file the questionnaire on the athletics
site the same day, because most programs enter the questionnaire into the database and never open the email.
Coach {name},
I am a {grade} class point guard at {high school} in {town}. I am {height}, {weight}, and I run
a {GPA} with {test line}. I averaged {PPG} points, {RPG} rebounds and {APG} assists in {games} varsity games
last winter ({source}); our team won {n} and made the {round}. I am also {n} in the {shot chart stat},
which is the part of my game I am trying to turn into a college role.
Film, {duration} minutes, defence included: {link}
Full games available on request.
I am looking at {division} programs where a guard can defend two positions and run an offense. {School} is on
my list because {one true, specific reason}. Could you tell me whether you have room in the roster limit for a
guard in {year}, and whether you would want a questionnaire?
Thank you for your time.
{first last} | {high school} {class} | {phone} | {email}
High-school coach: {name}, {phone}
The cadence. First contact on the day the division allows it. If there is no answer, one follow-up
after 12 to 14 days with one new thing in it: a weekend stat line, a better clip, a grade, an invitation to see you
play. Never "just checking in", never two emails in the same day. After a contact number exists, a short text every
four to six weeks is normal and expected; the phone number is yours to give once they ask for it.
The one-sheet: fields a coach will use
Name, position, height (barefoot in the off-season, and say which), weight, class year, eligibility number
High school, club program, jersey number and colour, and the town the film was shot in
GPA, test scores if you have them (NAIA still uses them), and course list status
Season stats with the source named, and the two or three numbers that describe your role rather than your ceiling
Film link, full-game link, athlete email and phone, high-school coach name and phone, parent contact
One honest line on what you want to study
Put no ranking on it. If a service ranks you 4,000th, that number will not change anyone's mind;
your defensive rebounding rate will.

The Commit Book · Basketball 5 · Grassroots and visits
5. Grassroots, visits, and the rulebook around your summer
The certification system
Division I coaches may evaluate non-scholastic basketball only at events and on teams that go through the NCAA
Basketball Certification System (Bylaw 13.10.4). That is where a grassroots program is built, where adults are
screened, and where a 16- or 17-year-old's non-parent host-family address creates extra paperwork. The permissible
windows are narrower than families expect and differ by sex: in the June men's window, coaches may evaluate from noon
Friday to 6pm Sunday; the women's June window runs noon Thursday to 6pm Saturday, with separate contact windows in
September, at national association events, and in April.
Ask the program, in writing, before you pay
Is this team and this event certified in the Basketball Certification System?
Which college coaches attended last year, by name and title, from the division I am targeting?
Where exactly is it broadcast, and does the film meet the elevated-camera standard in chapter four?
Who is the non-parent adult on my roster, and will the host-family documentation be filed?
Visits, and the rule nobody expects
Official (paid) visits open on the first date printed in that year's recruiting calendar and may not fall inside
an evaluation or dead period; each school may pay for one visit, and a school may host a maximum of five visitors at
an institutional money event at a time. There is no rule limiting how many times you may take an
unofficial visit or how much you may spend on it. One date bites families: in Division I an unofficial
visit is not permissible during the month of July unless the player has signed a written offer of admission or aid,
or paid an admissions deposit. The July scouting trip becomes a road trip; the coach cannot host you.
Dead periods are 24 to 26 December and the dates printed on each sport's calendar. In the 2026-27
men's calendar there is also a short dead period around the November signing window and one in late February. Nothing
is permissible in a dead period: no visits, no contact, no evaluations.

Six ways families waste money, in order of size
Paying for a showcase before a named coach confirms he will be there.
Buying the elite grassroots circuit for a body type the circuit does not target. The regional events are where
the D2, D3 and NAIA coaches, who are 61% of your doors, actually are.
Buying a recruiting service for the ranking it gives you. Ask instead how many coaches logged in last season.
Music, free throws, warm-up dunks, and offence-only film. Defence and full possessions are the cheapest edge in
the sport.
Parent-voiced emails. Coaches report deprioritising them, and several NAIA coaches say it out loud.
Waiting for a camp invitation you already received at a school that is already texting you. The second invitation
is not an evaluation; the first one was.

The Commit Book · Basketball 1 · Team limits
1. How many players a team can take
Every plan in this book comes from one question: how many players can a team carry, and how many of them can the
team pay for? In basketball the team is small and the number of players is huge, so the answer matters more here
than in most sports.
The rule today
What it means for your list
Fifteen players on the team. Aid is not capped and no one is promised more than one year
at a time. The old limit was 13 for men and 15 for women.
Ask how many of the fifteen will be paid next year, and whether one is set aside for your
position. "How many scholarships do you have" is the wrong question.
D1, other schools
No national team-size rule. The conference or the school sets the size.
Ask the same question. A coach who will not answer it is telling you something.
Ten full scholarships to spread across the whole team.
Most offers are for half or a third. Compare real cost, not reputation.
No money for sports at all.
The offer is about getting in, plus the aid the school gives for grades or need. The coach can speak up
for you but cannot pay you.
Eight scholarships. No calendar, no rules on when a coach may contact you, and no national letter program.
The lowest grade rules and the fastest coach contact. But the letter you sign does not protect you the
way you might think. Read what the school's own paper says.
Junior college
Fifteen scholarships, one school year at a time, and one letter that closes the door on other junior colleges.
A real second path. Your child can earn credits, play right away, and move up a year later.
There are 540,704 boys playing high school basketball. 3.6% reach any NCAA
school: 1.1% at Division I, 1.1% at Division II, and 1.5% at Division III. Across all high school sports, about
2% of athletes get any money for sports. Now count the doors the other way. Last year there were
1,187 first-year players at Division I, 988 at Division II, and 897 at Division III. 61% of those places
were at Division II and Division III. The NCAA prints both numbers. Most families have only seen the first one.
So how long should your list be?
Build your list around the schools you can really reach. For most players that means Division II, Division III,
NAIA, or junior college, with Division I as the bonus. A good starting list has all five levels on it:
8 to 12 Division I schools where you fit a position they need
10 to 15 Division II schools
10 to 15 Division III schools where the grades and the aid package work for your family
5 to 10 NAIA schools
3 to 5 junior college programs your child would really attend if nothing else came through
If your list is shorter than this, it is a hope, not a plan.

The Commit Book · Basketball 3 · The paperwork
3. What the school is really offering
"Aid" means money from the school that lowers what your family pays. Each level uses a different paper, and the
papers bind you in different ways.
The paper that counts
Earliest they can give it to you
Written offer of aid from the school. It may be the school's own form or a standard
one-page offer. Transfers sign a different paper.
On or after 1 August of senior year . Before that day the school may not put aid in writing.
It does not hold a spot on the team for you, and it goes away if you do not qualify in school.
Award letter, which is a formal financial aid document
It does not promise the same money next year. Most offers are written one year at a time.
The school's own aid letter plus your acceptance letter
With the acceptance letter. There is no sports aid paper at all.
A Division III coach may not even use a letter of intent. Nothing you sign holds you in place.
A letter of intent, but the NAIA does not enforce one
Any time. The NAIA has no calendar.
It gives you no national protection. Read what the school's paper says about backing out.
One letter of intent per sport, signed on 1 November
Binds your child for one school year
It does not stop a four-year school. It does close the door on every other junior college.
Four questions that turn "we like you" into a number
How many of the fifteen will be paid next year, and how many are set aside for my position?
Is there room for me on the team list you hand in this December, or does a player ahead of me have to leave?
What would have to be true for you to put the aid in writing on or after 1 August?
If I sign in November, what happens to my money in year two?
Coaches may answer questions one and two, and the new settlement rules say they may share roster numbers. A coach
who answers them is recruiting you. A coach who changes the subject is telling you where you sit on the list, and
that is worth more than a compliment.
Who sends it. The player, from the player's own email, with the high school coach copied. Coaches
rarely say it out loud, and NAIA coaches say it plainly: if a parent writes the email, the coach assumes the player
cannot read or write well. The parent's job is the paperwork and the dates, not the inbox.
The subject line. Class year, position, height, GPA, town, and one number that matters:

The email. Under 180 words, in the player's own words. One honest line on why this school. The
video link and the facts. One question. No attachments. Then fill out the sports form on the school's website the
same day. Many schools put the form in their system and never open the email.

The Commit Book · Basketball 5 · Summer and visits
5. Summer teams, visits, and the July rule
The summer team approval system
In Division I, a coach may only watch non-school basketball at events the NCAA has approved. The system is called
the Basketball Certification System. That is where a summer team is set up, where the adults are checked, and where
extra paperwork shows up if a player lives with a family that is not his own. The hours a coach may watch are
limited, and they differ for boys and girls: in June, men's coaches may watch from noon Friday to 6pm Sunday, and
women's coaches from noon Thursday to 6pm Saturday.
Ask the team these four things in writing, before you pay
Is this team and this event on the NCAA's approved list?
Which college coaches came last year? Names and job titles, please.
Where is it filmed, and does the video meet the camera standard in Chapter 4?
Who is the adult in charge of my child, and is that paperwork filed?
Visits, and the rule that surprises people
A paid visit is called an official visit. It is allowed starting on the date printed in that year's calendar, and
it may not fall inside a period when coaches are barred from contact. The school pays for one visit per school. A
school may host no more than five recruits at a time when it pays. There is no rule about how often you may take an
unofficial visit, or how much you spend on it. Now the one that hurts: in Division I, an unofficial
visit is not allowed during the month of July unless your child has already signed a written offer of aid or
admission, or paid a deposit to the school. The July trip becomes a road trip, because the coach cannot host you.
Dead periods are December 24 to 26, plus the dates printed on each sport's calendar. In the
2026-27 men's calendar there is also a short dead period around the November signing week and one in late February.
In a dead period nothing is allowed: no visits, no contact, no in-person ratings.

$250 to $950 per event, three to six times a year
Pay after a coach you can name says he will be there. In basketball most coaches watch at summer-team

$250 to over $6,000. The two biggest ones publish no price.
Ask how many college coaches actually logged in last season. A service gives you a page and a form. It
does not give you a relationship.

Phone on a tripod, free editing software, your school's own stream.

The real cost is the person who watches your games and picks clips: $450 to

A free profile page is not the same as approval. You need approval before a Division I official visit.
Standardized tests
$68 to $70, waivers available
The NCAA has not required a score for students starting college from 1 August 2023. The NAIA
still uses test scores , and many junior college and Division II offices do too.
A real total, spread over four years: $3,000 to $10,000 a year . Most of it is summer team fees,
travel, and video. Two ways to do it: handle it yourself for $700 to $2,000 a year (build the profile, keep the
classes on track, send the emails yourself, shoot your own video), or pay for help at $1,000 to $3,500 a year on top
of the camp money you were spending anyway. Either can lead to an offer. The difference is time and follow-through,
not rules.
Six ways families waste money, biggest first
Paying for a showcase before a coach you can name says he will be there.
Paying for the top summer circuit when your child is not the type they chase. Regional events are where the
Division II, Division III, and NAIA coaches are, and 61% of the places are with those coaches.
Paying a recruiting service for a ranking. Ask how many coaches logged in last season instead.
Music, free throws, warm-up dunks, and offense-only video. Defense and full possessions cost nothing and set
you apart.
Parent-written emails. Coaches say they give those less attention, and several NAIA coaches say it openly.
Waiting for a camp invite from a school that is already texting you. The first invite was the real one.
